title: From spaghetti to a platform
summary: Point-to-point links, the classic ESB, the modern integration platform, gateways and service meshes.

steps.title: The integration problem
body: **Acme Books** sells books online. It runs a shop website, a mobile app, a catalogue service, an order service,
a warehouse system, a billing system and a shipping carrier's API.
Each of them needs data from some of the others. The first way teams solve this is **point-to-point**: every
system calls every other system it needs, directly.
```text
shop ─── catalogue        shop ─── orders
app ─── warehouse ─── billing ─── carrier
With `n` systems all talking to each other that is `n × (n − 1) / 2` links. Every link has its own format,
its own authentication, its own error handling and its own owner. Change one system's format and every link
that touches it breaks. That tangle is called **integration spaghetti**.

steps.prompt: Acme Books has **8** systems and every pair is connected point-to-point. How many links is that?
steps.explain: `8 × 7 / 2 = 28`. Each link is a small piece of custom code that somebody must own, secure and monitor.

steps.title: Hubs, buses and platforms
body: The fix that became popular in the 2000s was a **hub**: every system connects once, to the middle, and the
middle translates. Commercial products called this an **Enterprise Service Bus (ESB)**.
- **ESB**: one central product that routes, transforms and orchestrates. It often grew into one giant
project owned by one team, holding business rules nobody else could see. Every change waited for that team,
and one bad deployment took down every integration at once. That is why "ESB" became a dirty word.
- **Integration platform** (the modern shape): the same patterns, but built as **many small integration
services**, one per business domain, with shared tooling and conventions, stored in Git, tested and
deployed independently. Apache Camel, MuleSoft, WSO2 Micro Integrator and Azure Logic Apps live here.
- **API gateway**: the front door for **consumers**. It decides *who* may call and *how often*. It is not
where integration logic lives.
> **Tip:** "ESB" today usually means *the integration layer*, not one monolithic product. Ask which one people mean.

steps.prompt: Match each term to what it is.
pairs: Each system calls each other system directly
One central product that routes and transforms for everyone
Many small, independently deployed integration services with shared conventions
The consumers' front door: authentication, subscriptions, rate limits
Sidecar proxies handling traffic between internal services

steps.title: North-south and east-west
body: Traffic is often described by direction:
- **North-south**: from outside (a partner, a phone app, a browser) into your platform. The **API gateway**
handles it: tokens, subscriptions, quotas, a developer portal.
- **East-west**: between your own services inside the platform. A **service mesh** (Istio, Linkerd)
handles it with a sidecar proxy next to every service: mutual TLS, retries, timeouts, traffic shifting,
telemetry.
Neither a gateway nor a mesh **transforms business data** or knows that a warehouse calls a book a `SKU` and the
shop calls it an `ISBN`. That translation is the integration layer's job.

items: The order service calls the warehouse service inside the cluster
The mobile app fetches a customer's orders
Mutual TLS between every pair of internal pods
A developer portal where partners request keys
Shifting 10% of internal traffic to a new version of the billing service

steps.prompt: Why did many classic ESB projects get a bad reputation?
options: Everything lived in one central project owned by one team, so changes queued up and one failure hit every integration
Routing messages between systems is an anti-pattern
Translating formats between systems is never needed
steps.explain: The patterns were fine. The organisation around them was not: one big shared deployable, one bottleneck team, business rules hidden in the middle.
Point-to-point grows with the square of the number of systems; a hub grows linearly.

steps.title: Count the cost of a change
prompt: - `int PointToPointLinks(int n)`: links needed when each of `n` systems connects to every other one.
- `int HubLinks(int n)`: links needed when each system connects once to a hub. With `0` or `1` systems there is nothing to connect, so return `0`.

- `int LinksToChange(int n, bool hub)`: one system changes its message format. How many links (integrations) must be updated? Point-to-point: every link touching that system. Hub: only that system's own link to the hub. Return `0` when `n < 2`.
hints: A system talks to `n - 1` others, and each link is shared by two systems.
With a hub, only the changed system's adapter to the hub needs work.
